title: Skill issue: Lessons from skilling up coding agents to use Langfuse - Marc Klingen, Clickhouse

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 50%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building and evaluating skills for coding agents (Claude Code) to add Langfuse instrumentation, with file-system diff evaluation and auto-research on the skill itself. Langfuse is a developer platform for observability and evaluation, and Claude Code is a coding assistant that consumes the skill. The talk covers skill development, LLM-as-judge evaluation over diffs, and distribution and versioning considerations. Assumes familiarity with coding agents, tracing, and evaluation but remains accessible to practitioners building similar skills. Conference case-study talk presenting six learnings from building a production skill for coding agents. Evidence is practitioner experience with live demonstrations, supported by transcript excerpts of grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Marc Klingen, co-founder of Langfuse, describes the open-source tracing and evaluation project as the largest in its space by tracked metrics, engineered out of Europe. He presents a conceptual mental model for agent skills using a Rubik's Cube analogy: skills provide the manual that sits between rigid workflows and fully autonomous agents, enabling progressive context fetching. The core problem is scale—478 documentation pages across five feature areas with heavy implementation flexibility due to Langfuse's deliberately un-opinionated infrastructure stance. Without a skill, Claude Code uses stale pre-training context, hallucinates removed methods, ships broken instrumentation, then fetches current docs; the resulting trace shows only two LLM calls with no visibility into agent actions. The skill uses SKILL.md for style guidance, progressive references to product modules, and a CLI wrapping existing APIs. Six learnings follow. Learning 1: inspecting traces gets roughly 80% of debugging detail; they instrumented Claude Code itself, discovering agents should determine data region explicitly and that advertising CLI help flags prevents hallucinated parameters. Learning 2: help agents navigate via an agent sitemap and content negotiation for markdown. Learning 3: surface a natural-language search endpoint backed by RAG so agents query directly. Learning 4: a basic eval setup using LLM-as-judge over file-system diffs is better than none; five eval templates were created. Learning 5: reference dynamic content rather than duplicating it, because duplicated content goes stale. Learning 6: auto-research loops on the skill itself, with a target function to migrate prompts into Langfuse prompt management; three of six suggested improvements were accepted, but the target function nearly backfired by optimizing out doc-fetching steps. Roadmap includes using skills for evaluation lifecycle automation—creating LLM-as-judge aligned with user preferences, analyzing user feedback patterns—bringing automation into product, and eventually an orchestration agent. In Q&A, Klingen notes the target function wasn't perfect, so human review of all suggestions was essential; the skill should feel like expert guidance. On distribution, he prefers auto-discoverable skills over plugin marketplaces (which require maintaining proprietary integrations for multiple vendors), and suggests timestamping skills so agents can detect staleness and fetch updates.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction to Marc Klingen and Langfuse
sections.summary: Marc Klingen introduces himself as a Langfuse co-founder, notes the project started 3 years ago, is the largest open-source project in its space by tracked metrics, and is engineered out of Europe.

sections.title: Conceptual mental model for agent skills
sections.summary: Klingen uses a Rubik's Cube analogy: a child has a bash tool but cannot solve the cube without the manual. Skills similarly give agents a reliable manual, sitting between rigid workflows and fully autonomous agents, enabling progressive context fetching for multi-domain problems.

sections.title: Tracing to discover use cases and improve skills
sections.summary: Tracing agent runtime helps identify unexpected user use cases that warrant new skills and reveals when existing skills are out of date or inefficient. Most teams now trace everything in the agent runtime.

sections.title: The problem: scaling documentation and onboarding for coding agents
sections.summary: Langfuse has 478 pages of documentation across five feature areas with heavy implementation flexibility due to its un-opinionated infrastructure stance. Without a skill, Claude Code uses stale pre-training context, hallucinates removed methods, ships broken instrumentation, catches the failure, then fetches current docs. The resulting trace shows only two LLM calls with no visibility into agent actions.

sections.title: Skill goal and structure
sections.summary: The goal is to give every Langfuse user an expert that helps quickly set up observability, instrumentation, and evals with best practices and up-to-date docs. The skill uses SKILL.md for style guidance and references to product modules for progressive disclosure, plus a CLI wrapping existing APIs so agents replicate manual UI workflows.

sections.title: Six learnings overview and Learning 1
sections.summary: Klingen introduces six learnings and covers Learning 1: inspecting traces gets you to roughly 80% of debugging detail. They instrumented Claude Code itself with Langfuse, interactively used the skill, and inspected traces to make the skill straight-shooting instead of wandering.

sections.title: Learning 1 details, Learning 2, and Learning 3
sections.summary: Practical sub-learnings from trace inspection: agents should determine the data region rather than defaulting to Europe, and the CLI help flag should be advertised to prevent hallucinated parameters. Learning 2: help agents navigate information via an agent sitemap and content negotiation—adding dot-MD to any docs page returns markdown, avoiding token-heavy HTML. Learning 3: surface a natural-language search endpoint backed by a RAG stack so agents query directly instead of fetching multiple pages; this also lets Langfuse track what problems users encounter and where docs need improvement.

sections.title: Learning 4 and Learning 5
sections.summary: Learning 4: a basic eval setup is better than none; they created five eval templates using natural-language statements evaluated by LLM-as-judge over file-system diffs before and after running the skill (e.g., checking OpenAI instrumentation was added and retrieval spans appear in traces). Learning 5: dynamic content should be referenced rather than duplicated, because duplicated content goes stale like pre-training context and creates yet another representation of Langfuse to maintain.

sections.title: Learning 6: Auto-research loops and target function pitfalls
sections.summary: Learning 6: auto-research applied to the skill itself, with a target function to migrate prompts from local Git repos into Langfuse prompt management. Three of six suggested improvements were accepted. However, the target function nearly backfired—minimizing turns led the optimizing agent to remove doc-fetching steps, negating the skill's reliability over time. Missing from the target function (e.g., linking prompt versions to production traces) meant the agent removed those steps as garbage.

sections.title: Discussion: distribution, versioning, and target function design
sections.summary: Challenges include no package management for skills (no staleness detection or auto-upgrade), manual installation gated by agent environments, and the tension between aiming for an initial aha moment versus a perfect setup that may overload users with questions. The skill is now the primary advertised way to set up Langfuse across all documentation. Klingen invites community feedback and notes weekly calls with users who increasingly prefer just asking their coding agent to handle setup.

sections.title: Roadmap and future outlook for agent automation
sections.summary: Klingen outlines a roadmap where skills help users get started and drive evaluation lifecycle automation—creating LLM-as-judge aligned with user preferences, analyzing patterns across user feedback on many executions, all fetched via CLI. The plan has three parts: automate via skills, bring automation into product, and build an orchestration agent that does what the team currently does manually.

sections.title: Q&A: human review, target function imperfection, and skill feel
sections.summary: Klingen clarifies that the auto-research target function wasn't perfect, producing many suggestions that didn't make sense, so all ideas were human-reviewed before changes were made. The goal is for the skill to feel like an expert user guiding you through what you need for your specific problem, offering professional guidance rather than generic recommendations.

sections.title: Q&A: skill distribution, plugin marketplaces, and timestamping
sections.summary: Asked about treating skills as packages or plugin marketplaces, Klingen says as a small team he's not excited about marketplaces because they require maintaining proprietary integrations across vendors (Anthropic, OpenAI, Cursor). He prefers auto-discoverable skills that agents find when needed, potentially without asking the user unless the skill is more trusted than the public web. For staleness, he suggests timestamping skills so agents can detect when a skill is old and fetch a fresh version, which would go a long way.
